text: Mehta Basti Ram was a Dogra officer and commander of the Fateh Shibji battalion under Raja Gulab Singh of Jammu (later Maharaja of Jammu and Kashmir). He joined Raja Gulab Singh's service in 1821, shortly after Gulab Singh conquered Kishtwar, and served under General Zorawar Singh during the conquest of Ladakh between 1834 and 1841. At the rank of Colonel, Basti Ram led Zorawar Singh's Jangi Fauj, which was later reorganised and renamed as the Fateh Shibji force from 1834 to 1841; this force became the 4th Battalion of the Jammu and Kashmir Rifles Regiment and retains the historic name Fateh Shibji. Major General G. D. Bakshi wrote in 2002 that Basti Ram was a "tactician par excellence" and that he "should be a role model for Indian battalion commanders". Basti Ram was a key officer in Zorawar Singh's forces and played a crucial role in the conquest of Ladakh, leading an attack that resulted in the capture of the Fort of Sod/Soth (in Kargil) and subsequently the Gyalpo, including crossing the Indus River on inflated goatskins. During the conquest of Baltistan, which began at the end of 1840, he devised a method to cross a river that had halted Zorawar Singh's army for over a month in cold and snow; for this innovation, Zorawar Singh gifted Basti Ram Rs. 500 and a pair of gold bangles. He was also present during the capture of Skardu. After capturing Western Tibet, Basti Ram was appointed governor of Taklakot (Burang), but when Tibetans launched a counterattack during winter, Zorawar Singh was killed on 12 December 1841 and his army was defeated; the troops at Taklakot fled to the British province of Kumaon, and Basti Ram escaped to Almora, where the British commissioner provided him shelter. By the autumn of 1846, he was appointed thanadar of Zanskar and "one of the confidential servants of Maharaja Gulab Singh". Basti Ram provided one of the earliest written accounts of the Dogra conquest of Ladakh and beyond, twelve years after the events; although the original version was lost, Alexander Cunningham re-wrote it based on a dictation by Basti Ram. August Hermann Francke noted that Basti Ram may have exaggerated enemy numbers at certain locations. Basti Ram was appointed thanadar of Leh between 1847 and 1861. At that time, there were four thanadars for Ladakh—Zanskar, Kargil, Dras, and Nubra—each with military and civil authority and directly accountable to the Maharaja. Alexander Cunningham estimated that Basti Ram's annual income was a "respectable" Rs. 18,000 (roughly £1,800 a year). Lieutenant Colonel Henry Torrens, who passed through Ladakh in 1862, noted that Basti Ram had retired to his home in Kishtawar due to old age and that no successor had been appointed by the Maharaja; instead, Torrens met the Kahlon of Leh, the "nominal governor", who received little respect from the Dogras. Basti Ram was born into the Mehta family of Kishtwar; his grandfather had been in charge of military affairs under the last Kishtwar ruler, Mohammad Teg Singh. His son, Mehta Mangal, succeeded him as Governor of Ladakh. Basti Ram's great-granddaughter was Krishna Mehta, who became the first woman member of parliament from Jammu and Kashmir. Krishna Mehta was married to Duni Chand Mehta, who was appointed wazir-e-wazarat of Muzaffarabad; Duni Chand was killed by Pashtun tribal militias in October 1947, and Krishna Mehta was taken prisoner and later repatriated by Pakistan. Krishna Mehta's brother Om Mehta served as Minister of State for Home Affairs in Indira Gandhi's government in 1976, and another younger brother, Ved Mehta, was at one time president of the Chamber of Commerce and Industry in Jammu.
